history.headline: Harold Vale's Reservoir Stilt Meets Sam Evers's Long Coat
history.text: Unconfirmed Reservoir Road animal report; residents debate names.

sam.belief: He saw a tall shape beside Reservoir Road after his bus route, but cannot explain what it was.
sam.stance: He still calls it The Long Coat and resents Harold and Ellen treating the name as a public joke. He is more uneasy than he lets on about passing the road again.

harold.belief: He has not seen the shape and has no firsthand idea what it was.
harold.stance: He still prefers The Reservoir Stilt and wants his name taken seriously, but worries the whole argument makes him look ridiculous.

ellen.belief: She has not seen the shape and does not claim to know what it was.
ellen.stance: She still prefers The Blank Sleeve. She thinks Harold is more concerned with protecting his pride than choosing a useful name, and she is willing to needle him about it.

public_record.headline: Sam Evers Wants Bramhollow to Call the Shape “The Long Coat”
Harold Vale Adds Two Rival Names to Bramhollow’s Coat Argument
Harold Vale's Reservoir Stilt Meets Sam Evers's Long Coat

turns.text: Sam, you’ve called it The Long Coat. Why that?
Because it was tall and narrow. That’s what I saw. I’m not dressing it up for Harold’s approval.
You’ve named a thing you can’t identify. That’s not naming, Sam. That’s hanging a coat on a fence.
You weren’t there.
No, I was at work, where people come in asking for nails instead of a bedtime story.
Harold, you sell screws by the inch and still manage to make every conversation about your own importance.
Thank you, Ellen. That’s almost a sentence.
It was a complete one. You may keep it.
Sam, what made you sure it was a shape and not something beside the road?
I don’t know what it was. I know where it stood. I keep remembering the exact patch of road, and that’s the bit I don’t like.
That’s a patch of road, not a name.
You could try shutting up long enough to hear what I’m saying.
I heard you. You want a name before anyone laughs.
I don’t care if they laugh.
You’ve said that three times, Sam. It sounds less convincing each time.
Harold, if you haven’t seen it, what exactly are you objecting to?
The name. It sounds like something left on a bus.
Then don’t pick it up.
Harold, The Reservoir Stilt. Why a stilt?
Tall. Reservoir. It’s got a spine to it, unlike a coat that’s apparently wandered off a bus.
You’re proud of that? You’ve named a thing you never saw after the nearest puddle.
Reservoir. Not puddle. Words do matter, Sam.
Harold has mistaken a longer word for a better thought.
And you’ve named it The Blank Sleeve. You’ve managed to make a sleeve sound unemployed.
It is a description, not a job reference.
Ellen, why that name?
It’s spare. The shape was tall, according to Sam; a sleeve suggests a person without pretending we know there was one.
I didn’t say sleeve. I said it was there.
Then we need a vote. A proper one. I’ll put a box by the register Saturday.
You’ll put a box by the register so every customer has to see you winning.
I’m open longer than you are. That’s called convenience.
It’s also called having your own ballot box beside the nails.
Sam, would a vote bother you?
The name doesn’t bother me. It’s that patch of road. I can still point to it without looking.
That doesn’t make it—
Don’t finish that for me.
Harold, you say your name sounds less foolish. Are you worried people are laughing at the name, or at you?
I’m worried you’re helping them do both. The Reservoir Stilt has a shape to it. The others sound like things Sam’s misplaced.
I haven’t misplaced anything. And I didn’t offer garden supplies so you could use me as your example of a town fool.
I didn’t say that. You’re the one making every sentence sound like a personal injury.
Harold, you could make a compliment sound like an invoice.
You’ve been waiting all week to say that.
No. I thought of it just now. It’s worse for you that way.
Sam, does the garden offer have anything to do with wanting the town to take you seriously?
It has to do with the garden needing supplies. That’s all. I don’t need a prize for lending things.
No, you just need everyone to call it The Long Coat.
I didn’t ask everyone to do anything. You’re the one trying to turn this into a contest.
A name is a contest the minute people start choosing sides.
Then stop standing there with a little flag in your hand.
I have no flag. I have a hardware store. People know what I sell.
I know what I saw. I don’t know what it was. Those aren’t the same thing.
When you pass Reservoir Road now, do you look for it?
No. I look away before I get there. Then I wonder why I did.
That still doesn’t make it a—
